newsitem.title: SHARJAH: Fuel surcharge in spotlight at Sharjah cargo meet.
newsitem.headline: Fuel surcharge in spotlight at Sharjah cargo meet.

text.p: The air freight fuel surcharge, and its scrapping by some airlines, is likely to come under the spotlight when industry executives meet at the Airports Council International (ACI) conference in Sharjah this weekend.

The surcharge, introduced last November by many airlines worldwide after jet fuel prices surged, will be under review at the meeting following recent moves by some airlines to drop the tariff in line with ebbing jet fuel costs.
Last week Virgin Atlantic said it would be lifting its surcharge from April 1 and United its effective April 7. On March 13 Delta Air Lines said it was removing its surcharge with immediate effect.

Alitalia North American marketing manager Ross Pizzillo has said the airline was waiting to see if jet fuel prices drop to the levels of last June before removing the surcharge. But he said if many other carriers remove their charges, Alitalia would follow suit.
Industry analysts say the rate at which the surcharge is scrapped is already slower than the pace at which it was introduced in the fourth quarter.

Between June and October last year jet fuel prices rose by more than 20 percent, prompting the surcharge and higher passenger air fares. But because of a mild winter in the West, oil prices have given up some of their post-Gulf War highs since the fourth quarter.

The cost of jet fuel since late-1996 has fallen by 30 percent, but as major airlines have been on a huge buying spree in the swaps market this year, they have locked in a price for next year of around $20 a tonne higher than recent prices, industry executives say.
Shippers are thus less likely to reap the benefit of a fall in jet fuel despite getting hit last autumn when they rose.

Apart from talk of surcharges, Sharjah, one of seven members of the United Arab Emirates, also hopes to sell the sea-air concept and lure more customers to set up hubs at its facility when it hosts the two-day ACI conference, starting on Sunday.

"We are marketing this hub concept and are talking to more airlines than before. Airlines usually follow each other and learn from each other," airport director general Ghanem al-Hajri told Reuters recently, hinting more airlines would follow the example of Lufthansa Cargo in setting up a Sharjah hub.

Air cargo, which represents around a third of world trade by value, is an important early indicator of a country's economic performance. ACI says freight and mail traffic handled by the 487 airports around the world in December 1996 totalled 4.48 million tonnes.

Reuters surveys show air cargo business from the United Arab Emirates has picked up since the end of the Ramadan fasting month and Eid festival which followed, and since Chinese New Year in the Far East.
Business from the Far East, mainly in the form of sea-air cargo, will likely be discussed in the ACI meeting's session on airports as intermodal cargo points.
Development of the sea-air freight business is something which Sharjah, which handled a total 320,000 tonnes of freight last year, claims credit for. "We really developed this concept," Hajri said.
Nearby Dubai is another example of intermodalism working for an airport.
Much of the cargo that moves through both these airports originates in the Far East, with final destination mainly Europe, the United States or states of the former Soviet Union.
Shipments -- particularly textiles -- are brought by sea from the Far East and Indian subcontinent, broken down into smaller packages, and sent by air worldwide.
Hajri said Central Asian states were increasingly becoming aware of the cost advantages of using Sharjah as a sea-air hub.

"Sea-air really solves the problem of getting goods to the central Asian states where there are no ports and roads are not very good. If you use sea-air via the UAE from the Far East to the CIS you can cut costs by almost 50 percent," Hajri says.
The Boeing World Air Cargo Forecast backs up this claim that the Middle East is now being considered as a major hub for air distribution into Russian and other CIS members.
The Middle East air freight market will grow at six percent annually between 1995 and 2015, compared to a worldwide average
